197 FERC ¶ 61,014
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Before Commissioners:  Laura V. Swett, Chairman;
                                        David Rosner, Lindsay S. See,
                                        Judy W. Chang, and David LaCerte.


ORDER ADDRESSING ARGUMENTS RAISED ON REHEARING AND CLARIFICATION, SETTING ASIDE PRIOR ORDER, IN PART, AND
ESTABLISHING HEARING AND SETTLEMENT JUDGE PROCEDURES

(Issued October 7, 2026)

On March 6, 2026, the Commission issued an order in response to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit’s (D.C. Circuit, or court) remand of the Commission’s order on the above-captioned complaints.  As relevant here, the Commission in the Order on Remand found that the de minimis threshold provision of the solution-based distribution factor (DFAX) method was unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory, directed PJM to eliminate the de minimis threshold, and denied a separate complaint filed by Neptune Regional Transmission System, LLC (Neptune) and Long Island Power Authority, L.L.C. (LIPA) in Docket     No. EL21-39-000 regarding PJM’s practice of netting under the solution-based DFAX method.  The Commission also established paper hearing procedures regarding the application of the solution-based DFAX method to the assignment of cost responsibility for transmission facilities that address short circuit reliability concerns.
Timely requests for rehearing and clarification were filed by the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC), Neptune and LIPA (Neptune/LIPA), and PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (PJM).  Timely requests for rehearing were filed by East Kentucky Power Cooperative, Inc. (EKPC) and PJM Indicated Transmission Owners.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners filed an errata to their rehearing request on April 7, 2026.  
Pursuant to Allegheny Defense Project v. FERC, the rehearing requests filed in this proceeding may be deemed denied by operation of law.  However, as permitted by section 313(a) of the FPA, we are modifying the discussion in the Order on Remand and setting aside the order, in part, as discussed below.  We also grant, in part, and deny, in part, the requests for clarification, and establish hearing and settlement judge procedures, as discussed below.
Specifically, we continue to find, as further discussed below, that:  (1) PJM must recalculate the cost responsibility assignments for the Transmission Enhancement Charges for the period beginning June 18, 2015 to reflect the elimination of the                     de minimis threshold; (2) PJM must assess refunds and surcharges, including interest, to relevant entities; and (3) PJM’s practice of netting the flow of electricity remains just and reasonable.  We set the Order on Remand aside, in part, however, to remove the directive requiring PJM to update the historical Tariff records (each of the Tariff, Schedule 12 Appendices that became effective on or after June 18, 2015).  Additionally, we grant in part, and set for hearing, in part, certain of PJM’s requested clarifications pertaining to how to calculate the refunds and surcharges for settlement and hearing judge procedures along with the short circuit issues which were formerly set for paper hearing procedures.
Background
Technical Background
Background on DFAX, DFAX Values and de minimis Threshold 
PJM is the regional transmission organization responsible for coordinating the transmission of electricity in the mid-Atlantic region, which stretches from North Carolina to New Jersey.  
PJM files cost responsibility assignments for transmission projects that the PJM Board approves as part of PJM’s Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (RTEP) in accordance with Schedule 12 of PJM’s Tariff and Schedule 6 of the Operating Agreement.  Schedule 12 of the Tariff establishes Transmission Enhancement Charges for “[o]ne or more of the Transmission Owners [that] may be designated to construct and own and/or finance Required Transmission Enhancements by:  (1) the PJM RTEP periodically developed pursuant to Operating Agreement, Schedule 6; or (2) any joint planning or coordination agreement between PJM and another region or transmission planning authority set forth in Tariff, Schedule 12-Appendix B.”
In developing the RTEP, PJM identifies transmission projects to address different criteria, including PJM planning procedures, North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) Reliability Standards, Regional Entity reliability principles and standards, and individual transmission owner Form No. 715 local planning criteria.  Types of Reliability Projects identified in the RTEP include Regional Facilities, Necessary Lower Voltage Facilities, and Lower Voltage Facilities.
PJM uses a hybrid cost allocation method, which the Commission found complies with Order No. 1000, for Regional Facilities and Necessary Lower Voltage Facilities that address a reliability need.  Under this method, PJM allocates 50% of the costs of Regional Facilities or Necessary Lower Voltage Facilities on a load-ratio share basis and the other 50% based on the solution-based DFAX method.  PJM allocates all of the costs of Lower Voltage Facilities that are Reliability Projects using the solution-based DFAX method.  Cost responsibility assignments pursuant to the Order No. 1000-compliant cost allocation method are included in Schedule 12-Appendix A of the Tariff.
With respect to transmission expansions or enhancements for which costs are assigned using the solution-based DFAX method, PJM makes a preliminary cost responsibility determination for each Required Transmission Enhancement at the time such Required Transmission Enhancement is included in the RTEP.  Specifically, beginning with the calendar year in which a Required Transmission Enhancement is scheduled to enter service, and thereafter annually at the beginning of each calendar year, PJM updates the preliminary cost responsibility determination for each Required Transmission Enhancement using the values and inputs used in the base case of the most recent RTEP approved by the PJM Board prior to the date of the update.  All values and inputs used in the calculation of the DFAX in a determination of cost responsibility are the same values and inputs as used in the base case of the most recent RTEP approved by the PJM Board prior to the determination of cost responsibility. 
Relying on proprietary software, the solution-based DFAX method models how electricity will flow across a new transmission facility at moments of peak transmission system use (i.e., at “peak load”), and assigns costs proportionally, based on the projected use of the facility by utilities in each “zone” of PJM.  PJM recalculates the cost allocation of regional transmission plan projects over several years, to account for utilities’ evolving use of the transmission facilities.  
More specifically, PJM calculates DFAX values (represented as a decimal value) for each transmission facility.  This decimal value represents the change in flow on the transmission facility that would result from an increase in load of one megawatt (MW) in a given load zone during peak load, steady-state conditions, while holding load in all other load zones constant.  After calculating a DFAX value for each load zone, PJM would then apply a 1% de minimis threshold to the calculated DFAX values and replaces any DFAX value less than 1% with a DFAX value of zero.  This means that zones with a DFAX value below the 1% de minimis threshold are not included in the solution-based DFAX method results, known as the de minimis threshold.
Netting
Netting is a process by which PJM offsets positive and negative energy flows in calculating the total flow of electricity attributable to a zone under the solution-based DFAX method.  Electricity can flow in both positive and negative directions based on a point of reference such as a monitored facility or constraint.  A positive value is assigned for electricity flowing in the positive direction and a negative value is assigned for electricity flowing in the negative direction.  Under the solution-based DFAX method, PJM models the transfer of the net of energy flow in the positive and negative directions from all generation within a zone to all load within a transmission zone.  PJM then nets the positive and negative flows before calculating the DFAX value of the zone.  
Procedural History
This order addresses several separate proceedings dating back to 2015, all of which have overlapping or related legal issues.  Because the procedural history is extensive, we summarize only key points here; a more detailed description of the dockets and proceedings appears in the Order on Remand and preceding orders.
Con Edison and Linden Complaints
On November 7, 2014, Con Edison filed a complaint requesting that the Commission find unjust and unreasonable the solution-based DFAX method, particularly as PJM used that methodology to allocate the costs for the Bergen-Linden Corridor and Sewaren Projects.  Separately, on May 22, 2015, Linden filed the Linden Complaint to challenge the cost allocations as related to the same projects, arguing that the               solution-based DFAX method – including the de minimis threshold, and netting provisions – produces unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory and preferential results.  On June 18, 2015, the Commission denied the Con Edison Complaint, and on April 22, 2016, denied the Linden Complaint.
On February 8, 2017, PJM submitted revisions to Schedule 12-Appendix and Schedule 12-Appendix A of the PJM Tariff to revise cost responsibility assignments for transmission enhancements and expansions included in the PJM RTEP resulting from Con Edison’s termination of its Transmission Service Agreements (TSA), which the Commission accepted.  As a result of the termination of those agreements, the costs allocated to the Linden and Hudson Transmission Partners, LLC (Hudson) transmission owners increased under the solution-based DFAX allocation method.  On April 28, 2017, Linden submitted a second complaint against PJM (Second Linden Complaint) with respect to these revised cost responsibility assignments.  On February 20, 2020, the Commission denied the Second Linden Complaint.
Artificial Island Complaint
On August 28, 2015, pursuant to FPA section 205, PJM filed revisions to   Schedule 12-Appendix A to assign cost responsibility for projects that addressed stability limits on generation in southern New Jersey (Artificial Island Project).  Delaware and Maryland filed complaints arguing that PJM’s use of the solution-based DFAX method for the Artificial Island Project was unjust and unreasonable.  The Commission initially upheld the cost allocations and denied the complaint. 
On rehearing, the Commission found PJM’s use of the solution-based DFAX method to allocate costs of transmission facilities addressing stability constraints to be unjust and unreasonable.
Remand Opinion 
In the Remand Opinion, the D.C. Circuit held that the Commission failed to explain why the solution-based DFAX method was appropriate for allocating the costs of the Bergen-Linden Corridor and Sewaren short-circuit projects when, in the contemporaneous Artificial Island proceeding, it had rejected the solution-based DFAX method for a similar non-flow-based stability project.  The court pointed to the Commission’s finding that short-circuit projects also are not flow-based (i.e., a non-flow based constraint is a constraint that “is not caused by excessive demand”).  
The D.C. Circuit also ruled that PJM’s de minimis threshold—which exempted zones with less than a 1% distribution factor from any cost responsibility—violated the cost-causation principle and resulted in undue discrimination.  The D.C. Circuit found that the threshold effectively operated as a “too-big-to-pay” rule, allowing large utilities such as Public Service Electric and Gas (PSEG) to avoid costs despite receiving substantial benefits, while imposing nearly all costs on smaller entities such as merchant transmission providers.  The D.C. Circuit vacated the Commission’s prior determinations upholding the use of the de minimis threshold.  More specifically, the court found that distribution factors “measure a zone’s use of a facility relative to its total load” and, as a result, “the de minimis exception depends on the size of the zone, not on the zone’s share of the facility’s total flow.”  Under such a methodology, the court found, the de minimis threshold exempts large zones from cost allocation even though the zone may use a substantial percentage of the total flow on the facility.  The court held that the de minimis threshold violates the cost causation principle because it “exempts zones from bearing any costs based on their load size—a quality unrelated to the burdens they impose on or the benefits they receive from any individual facility,” and also “unduly discriminates against small zones,” which are allocated more costs when larger zones are exempted.  Consequently, the court concluded that the de minimis threshold  “cannot be considered just and reasonable” and is “unlawful.”
By contrast, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Commission’s finding that netting of positive and negative flows at delivery points was not unjust and unreasonable, finding that counterflows increase available transmission capacity and may appropriately reduce a zone’s cost responsibility.  
Additionally, the D.C. Circuit upheld the Commission’s finding that Con Edison was not obliged to continue to pay project costs after it ceased receiving service upon the termination of a power exchange transmission service agreement.  The D.C. Circuit vacated and remanded the orders for further proceedings on:  (1) the treatment of non-flow-based projects relative to Artificial Island (short-circuit issues); and (2) the            de minimis threshold, while leaving the remaining section 205 approvals in place.
Neptune/LIPA Complaint, PJM Indicated Transmission Owner Proceedings and Proposed Settlement
On December 31, 2020, Neptune/LIPA, pursuant to section 206 of the FPA, filed the Neptune/LIPA Complaint challenging certain provisions of the PJM Tariff for the portion of cost responsibility that is assigned pursuant to the solution-based DFAX method.  On June 25, 2021, the Commission established paper hearing procedures to develop a further record.  
On April 11, 2022, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners, pursuant to section 205 of the FPA, filed the Host Zone Proposal, which proposed revisions to Schedule 12 of the PJM Tariff to provide that the de minimis threshold would not apply to the zone in which the relevant transmission facility is located, but would continue to apply to other zones.
On June 10, 2022, the Commission accepted and suspended the Host Zone Proposal and established paper hearing procedures.  Because the Host Zone Proposal proceeding and the Neptune/LIPA Complaint proceeding both addressed the de minimis threshold provision of the solution-based DFAX method, and involved common issues of law and fact, the Commission consolidated the proceedings (Consolidated Proceedings).
On February 14, 2025, the Settling Parties filed a proposed settlement of the Consolidated Proceedings (Settlement Proposal).  The Settlement contains two components.  First, like the PJM Transmission Owners’ Host Zone Proposal, the Settlement proposed to eliminate the de minimis threshold only for the zone where a transmission facility is located, and includes clarifications to ensure appropriate application of the Host Zone Proposal based on the information available to PJM at the time a project is approved by PJM.  Second, the Settlement provided that certain merchant transmission facilities will no longer be treated as separate PJM zones for purposes of calculating cost assignments under the solution-based DFAX method.  Instead, pursuant to the Settlement Proposal and the accompanying Tariff revisions, these merchant transmission facilities would be treated comparable to load in the PJM zone with which they are interconnected for purposes of determining their responsibility under the solution-based DFAX method.
Order on Remand
As relevant here, the Commission in the Order on Remand found that the                     de minimis threshold is unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory and thus modified the vacated and remanded prior orders on the Con Edison Complaint in Docket No. EL15-18-005, Linden Complaint in Docket No. EL15-67-005, Second Linden Complaint in Docket No. EL17-68-003 and granted the Neptune/LIPA Complaint in Docket No. EL21-39-000 on that issue.  On remand, the Commission found that the           de minimis threshold from cost allocation under the solution-based DFAX method results in an assignment of cost responsibility that is unjust and unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory because it distorts a zone’s use of a facility by multiplying the DFAX value by the peak zonal load.  
In establishing a just and reasonable replacement rate, the Commission first considered and rejected the Host Zone Proposal submitted by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and the Settlement Proposal because these each included modifications to the de minimis threshold, under which the existing de minimis threshold would not apply to the zone in which the relevant transmission facility is located but would continue to apply to other zones.  As such, the Commission found these alternative proposals raised the same concerns about cost causation that the court identified with regard to the existing de minimis threshold.
Instead, the Commission found that the just and reasonable replacement rate supported by the record in this proceeding is the elimination of the de minimis threshold.  The Commission concluded that “[e]liminating the de minimis threshold exemption results in cost allocations based on relative usage of the transmission facility as determined via the solution-based DFAX method without exemptions that distort the cost allocation.”
  The Commission also established paper hearing procedures to obtain additional record evidence to address the concerns raised in the Remand Opinion regarding the application of the solution-based DFAX method to transmission facilities that address short circuit reliability violations.  The Commission denied the Neptune/LIPA Complaint on the issue of netting, for the same reasons discussed in prior orders on the Con Edison and Linden Complaints, as affirmed in the Remand Opinion.  In addition, the Commission affirmed the determination in the order in Docket No. ER17-950-006 providing for the reallocation of cost responsibility following termination of the Con Edison TSAs.  Finally, the Commission directed PJM to correct its billing and provide relief for all projects subject to the solution-based DFAX cost allocation method back to June 18, 2015 and provide refunds within 90 days of the Order on Remand.
Notice of Extension of Time 
PJM’s request for rehearing also included a request for an extension of time to comply with the Commission’s directives to recalculate the cost responsibility assignments of projects and resettle billings for those projects.  On April 29, 2026, the Commission granted PJM’s request for an extension of time.  Specifically, the Commission extended the time “to recalculate the cost allocations in Schedule 12 and correct the billing (with interest calculated pursuant to section 35.19(a) of the Commission regulations)” for all projects subject to the solution-based DFAX cost allocation method back to June 18, 2015, “to make cleanup filings through eTariff to correct the cost allocations for each cost allocation,” and to refile revised, historical versions of Schedule 12 of the Tariff until further order of the Commission.  The Commission directed PJM to comply with all other directives of the Order on Remand, including revising Schedule 12 to eliminate the de minimis threshold prospectively by filing a revised version of the currently effective Schedule 12.   
Discussion
Procedural Issues
Answers
On April 20, 2026, Neptune/LIPA, the Public Service Electric and Gas Company, and New York Entities filed separate motions for leave to answer and answers to PJM’s Motion for Clarification and Rehearing and PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ request for rehearing.  On April 21, 2026, the Delaware Public Service Commission filed an answer in support of other requests for rehearing and clarification.  On April 22, 2026, the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities and the New Jersey Division of Rate Counsel filed an answer to PJM’s rehearing request.  On May 13, 2026, the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission filed comments in support of the requests for rehearing and clarification.  
Rule 713(d) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure prohibits an answer to a request for rehearing.  Accordingly, we deny the motions for leave to answer and reject the answers.
Motions to Intervene
On April 8, 2026, the Kentucky Attorney General filed a motion to intervene out of time.  On April 9, 2026, Wolverine Power Supply Cooperative, Inc. (Wolverine) filed a motion to intervene out of time.  On April 21, 2026, the Delaware Division of the Public Advocate (DPA) filed a motion to intervene out of time.  On June 12, 2026, Buckeye Power, Inc. (Buckeye) filed a motion to intervene out of time.  On July 2, 2026, pro se merchant transmission developer, Adam Rouselle, filed a motion to intervene out of time, a request for official notice of other Commission dockets, a request to admit new material record evidence, a request for expedited remedial treatment, and comments.  On July 17, 2026, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners filed an answer in opposition to     Mr. Rouselle’s motion to intervene, and Mr. Rousselle filed a motion for leave to answer and answer to PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ response on July 21, 2026.  
Pursuant to Rule 214(d) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, we deny movants’ motions to intervene out-of-time.  In ruling on a motion to intervene out-of-time, we apply the criteria set forth in Rule 214(d), and consider, among other things, whether the movant had good cause for failing to file the motion within the time prescribed.  When, as here, late intervention is sought after the issuance of a dispositive order, the prejudice to other parties and burden upon the Commission of granting the late intervention may be substantial.  Thus, the movant bears a higher burden to demonstrate good cause for granting such late intervention.  
Here, Buckeye and Wolverine offer no explanation for their delay in moving to intervene.  DPA argues it only recently became aware of “the Commission’s rules regarding this matter.”  Mr. Rouselle argues that the Order on Remand addresses DFAX cost causation issues that relate to the same historical period as proceedings in Docket No. EL15-794 and Docket No. EL26-40.  These proceedings have been ongoing for over 11 years—including review by the D.C. Circuit and an Order on Remand—and throughout that time DFAX cost causation matters were unambiguously at issue.  None of the movants have offered a compelling explanation for why their motions could not have been timely filed; therefore, we find that movants have failed to demonstrate the requisite good cause, and we deny the motions to intervene out-of-time.
Statement of Issues
EKPC’s rehearing request is deficient because it fails to include a Statement of Issues section separate from its arguments, as required by Rule 713 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure.  Rule 713(c)(2) requires that a rehearing request must include a separate section entitled “Statement of Issues” listing each issue presented to the Commission in a separately enumerated paragraph that includes representative Commission and court precedent on which the participant is relying.  Under Rule 713, any issue not so listed will be deemed waived.  Accordingly, we reject EKPC’s rehearing request.  Nevertheless, to provide clarity, we address EKPC’s arguments below.
New Evidence
We reject the declaration appended to PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ rehearing request as an attempt to add evidence to the record purporting to estimate the size of the refunds that would result from reallocating costs following the elimination of the de minimis threshold.  Under longstanding precedent, we do not consider arguments or new evidence raised for the first time on rehearing, subject to a narrow exception for matters that could not have been previously presented, e.g., claims based on information that only recently became available or concerns prompted by a change in material circumstances.  We have adopted this approach “because (1) our regulations preclude other parties from responding to a request for rehearing and (2) such behavior is disruptive to the administrative process because it has the effect of moving the target for parties seeking a final administrative decision.”  Here, the parties have had previous opportunities to provide such evidence, including when PJM Indicated Transmission Owners previously argued against eliminating the de minimis threshold.  For the same reasons, we likewise reject PJM’s inclusion of additional declarations providing new evidence regarding the impact of refunds to the extent they support PJM’s request for rehearing.
Substantive Issues 
De minimis Threshold
Rehearing and Clarification Requests
As discussed in greater detail below, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and EKPC argue on rehearing that the Commission erred in selecting a replacement rate that entirely eliminated the existing de minimis threshold and in failing to adequately consider alternative replacement rates.  In addition, Neptune/LIPA seek clarification that the prior inclusion of a MW usage-based de minimis threshold as a part of a proposed remedy for the Neptune/LIPA Complaint does not preclude a future proposal of a prospective MW usage-based de minimis threshold for application within the DFAX cost allocation assignment procedure.
Commission Determination
As discussed below, we continue to find that eliminating the de minimis threshold is the just and reasonable replacement rate in this proceeding.  The D.C. Circuit concluded that the existing de minimis threshold contained in PJM’s Tariff violated the cost causation principle and caused undue discrimination because smaller zones were required to absorb higher costs when larger zones are exempted based on their “use of a facility relative to their total load.”  As discussed in the Order on Remand, the alternative proposals put forward by the parties do not cure these concerns.  By contrast, eliminating the de minimis threshold ensures that the cost allocation under PJM’s solution-based DFAX method is roughly commensurate with the benefits that zones receive from their use of the facilities.  None of the arguments raised on rehearing convince us that this analysis was in error. 
Consideration of Alternative Proposals
Rehearing Request 
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that the D.C. Circuit in the Remand Opinion did not require the Commission to eliminate any version of the 1% DFAX        de minimis threshold on remand.  Rather, they claim the D.C. Circuit merely rejected the then-effective DFAX-based 1% de minimis threshold and remanded for “further proceedings.”  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend this outcome left open the possibility that the Commission could modify the de minimis threshold to address the D.C. Circuit’s concerns rather than eliminate the de minimis threshold altogether.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that the Commission failed to adequately consider options beyond elimination of the de minimis threshold to address the concerns identified by the D.C. Circuit despite various parties submitting pleadings regarding appropriate procedure on remand.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners note that the Commission set the short circuit issues, which also were remanded for further proceedings, for paper hearing.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that the Commission considered additional evidence in the Neptune/LIPA Complaint proceeding, but failed to consider evidence presented by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners that they claim demonstrates that removing the de minimis threshold would harm customers in smaller zones relative to customers in larger zones.  They state that the Commission additionally failed to consider the impacts of the Host Zone Proposal and the Settlement Proposal in eliminating the de minimis threshold.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners claim that the remedy provided by the Commission—reallocation of all PJM transmission projects in all zones going back to 2015—goes beyond the relief sought by the parties who brought the appeal.  They claim that the entities involved did not serve load in PJM but rather exported power from PJM to New York, and only sought relief for themselves and their New York customers.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that they offered a just and reasonable solution in the Settlement Proposal to address the New York exporters’ concerns, including providing that parties in their situation would be treated comparably to load in the PJM zone with which they are interconnected for purposes of the calculation of DFAX cost allocation assignments.
Commission Determination
We disagree with PJM Indicated Transmission Owners that the Commission failed to adequately consider options beyond elimination of the de minimis threshold.  The Commission considered comments, evidence, and alternative proposals put forward by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and other parties addressing the court’s conclusions on the de minimis threshold.   
Further, the Commission did not find in the Order on Remand that “the D.C. Circuit mandated the absolute elimination of the 1% de minimis threshold.”  Consistent with this view, the Commission considered alternatives to eliminating the 1% DFAX            de minimis threshold—including the Host Zone Proposal by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and the proposal reflected in the Settlement—before making a determination.  While the Commission ultimately rejected these alternative proposals, it did not do so based on a perceived imperative to eliminate the de minimis threshold outright.  Rather, the Commission rejected the alternative proposals because they raised the same concerns about cost causation that the D.C. Circuit identified regarding the previous de minimis threshold.  In particular, the Commission found that the alternative proposals, which each would continue to apply the de minimis threshold to zones other than the zone where the transmission facility is located, failed to address the court’s concerns by continuing to exempt zones based on their “use of a facility relative to their total load,” disproportionately benefiting larger zones. 
We are similarly not persuaded that the Commission failed to engage in “further proceedings” before eliminating the de minimis threshold, or that it was obligated to take the same action it took with respect to the short circuit issues.  The D.C. Circuit prescribed no specific process requirements in remanding issues for “further proceedings” and the Commission “has discretion regarding the process for deciding the issues before it and does not need to hold a hearing where, as here, it can resolve disputes on the basis of the record before it.”  Here, the Commission concluded that additional information was necessary to decide whether the solution-based DFAX method was unjust and unreasonable for the short circuit issues but no further information was necessary to determine a replacement rate for the de minimis threshold, particularly given the extensive record in this proceeding, including a technical conference and comments filed in that proceeding and PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ filing of the Host Zone Proposal and Settlement Proposal.  Contrary to PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ suggestion, the mere fact that the Commission set certain issues for hearing does not require it to do so for other issues.
We are not convinced by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ suggestion that the Commission should have held further hearings because the Commission was not prohibited from doing so by the D.C. Circuit.  Even in calling for further process with respect to selecting a replacement rate, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners do not explain what additional, relevant information is likely to be produced through a paper hearing.  Moreover, under the FPA, once the Commission finds a rate unjust and unreasonable, it is required to establish a just and reasonable replacement rate.  Given the court remand and the record before it, the Commission found that the elimination of the de minimis threshold was a just and reasonable result, as such elimination resulted in costs being allocated to zones based on their use of the project.  It also considered the alternative proposal by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and found that proposal was unjust and unreasonable.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners are free under FPA section 205 to propose another approach, but given the extensive filings here, the Commission was justified in finding that the elimination of the de minimis threshold created a just and reasonable result and did not need to investigate any and all possible alternatives to determine if they might be superior.
Nor are we convinced that the selected replacement rate was an overbroad remedy because the parties who brought the appeal only sought relief for themselves and their customers in New York, and their concerns could be addressed by the more limited proposal contained in the Settlement Proposal.  Even assuming that the Settlement Proposal would have addressed the New York exporters’ concerns, that alone would not satisfy the Commission’s statutory obligation to set a just and reasonable replacement rate, and one that addresses the court’s concerns.  In fact, the court’s concerns with the existing de minimis threshold were not limited to its application to specific transmission projects and zones with unique characteristics.  Rather, the court explicitly concluded that the existing de minimis threshold in PJM’s Tariff was unlawful.  To be responsive to this finding, the Commission appropriately established a just and reasonable replacement rate that eliminated the existing de minimis threshold for all zones.
Sufficiency of Evidence
Rehearing Requests
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that the Commission failed to consider PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ evidence of harm that would be caused by removing the de minimis threshold entirely and proposed alternatives to address the flaws in the de minimis threshold’s application.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that, in finding the previous            de minimis threshold unreasonable, the Remand Opinion was primarily concerned with customers in smaller zones being discriminated against when compared with customers in larger zones.  They claim this ruling was based on a limited record that primarily related to the impact on the New York Entities, a group that solely exported power from PJM to New York.  They claim that the Remand Opinion concerned only costs related to two projects in one PJM zone—the Bergen-Linden Corridor and Sewaren Projects in the PSEG zone—which the New York Entities asserted should be allocated to customers in the PSEG zone.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that the D.C. Circuit’s record did not represent other situations within the PJM transmission system.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners claim the refund time period that would apply to the       New York Entities’ claims was limited and fixed because the relevant entities did not have liability for these projects after termination of their TSAs effective December 31, 2017.
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners maintain that, given the limited scope of the record on appeal, the Commission’s ruling requiring reallocation of all past RTEP costs and the prospective allocation of all RTEP costs to customers in PJM zones was unduly broad.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that they provided evidence showing no consistent pattern of discrimination in smaller zones when compared with traditional zones, and that in most cases removing the de minimis threshold would adversely impact customers in smaller zones via a “substantial increase in costs.”  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners cite, as an example, their analysis of the impact of eliminating the de minimis threshold on customers in the Dayton Power & Light Company zone, which PJM Indicated Transmission Owners characterize as “relatively small.”  They claim these customers would see cost increases of 590% in 2020, 207% in 2021, and 224% in 2022 as a result of removal of the threshold.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and EKPC both point to the EKPC zone, another smaller zone, which they claim would see cost increases of 221% in 2020 and 83% in 2022.  EKPC argues that this snapshot of reallocations does not capture all the potential adverse impacts given that it only looks at data from 2020-2022, ignores interest, and uses various simplifying assumptions.  EKPC states that, as an electric cooperative, any adverse impact will be felt exclusively by retail customers rather than shareholders.  EKPC suggests that such adverse impact would be particularly acute because the covered territories include poor and rural areas.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that these cost shifts demonstrate that the Commission failed to select a just and reasonable replacement rate after finding the existing rate unjust and reasonable.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners claim cost increases would also be seen in other smaller zones, such as Duquesne and Metropolitan Edison Company, for some or all of the years between 2020 and 2022.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners suggest that the D.C. Circuit did not have this information to consider when reaching its conclusions, but that the Commission was provided with this information before the Order on Remand.  Because of this disparity of information, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners reason, the Commission may not rely on the D.C. Circuit’s conclusions that the de minimis threshold disproportionately favors larger over smaller zones.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that the Commission fails to recognize that the de minimis threshold is only a single component of the solution-based DFAX method, which involves many steps that interact with the topology of the PJM system.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners suggest that the Commission may not rely on hypothetical application of the de minimis threshold, but rather must look to the impacts of the application of the de minimis threshold, when record evidence shows that eliminating the de minimis threshold would, in practice, negatively impact the costs of consumers in smaller zones.    
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners further claim that the Commission erred in relying on evidence provided by Neptune/LIPA showing that in 2022 costs for 132 of 291 transmission facilities were allocated only to the host zone rather than an assignment of cost responsibility based on usage identified by the solution-based DFAX method.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners suggest this outcome is unsurprising given the relatively small scope of many transmission projects in PJM, such that they are unlikely to have impacts in other zones.  Further, they argue that the Commission failed to show that other zones benefit from such projects.
Commission Determination
Contrary to PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ suggestion, the Commission fully considered the evidence provided by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and found it insufficient to support adopting the two alternative replacement rates preferred by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners.  After examining this evidence, the Commission found that the alternative proposals raised the same concerns about cost causation that the D.C. Circuit identified regarding PJM’s existing de minimis threshold.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ and EKPC’s arguments in favor of the alternative replacement rates seek to relitigate whether the “perceived flaws” of the existing de minimis threshold were real, including whether the existing de minimis threshold actually discriminated against smaller zones.  Such claims are misplaced, as the court unequivocally concluded that “[b]ecause the de minimis threshold regularly produces ‘wholesale departure[s] from the cost-causation principle,’ it cannot be considered just and reasonable” without cabining this finding to particular parties, projects, or time frames with unique characteristics.  The Commission in the Order on Remand recognized that the elimination of the de minimis threshold may result in increases in cost allocation to some smaller zones, but agreed with the court that “because the PJM methodology multiplies the DFAX value by the peak load of the zone, it has a disproportionate effect on zones depending on their size.”  
Regardless, we do not find PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ and EKPC’s attempts to refute the court’s and the Commission’s findings persuasive.  We continue to find that, even if PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and EKPC are correct that the elimination of the de minimis threshold may result in increases in cost allocation to some smaller zones in certain instances, that does not undermine the court’s conclusion that, ceteris paribus, the de minimis threshold disproportionately favors larger over smaller zones.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and EKPC provide no evidence that the elimination of the de minimis threshold systematically favors larger zones.  Indeed, the record in this proceeding showed that the de minimis threshold increased costs significantly to much smaller zones, including Hudson, Neptune, and Linden.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners rely on a snapshot of only three years of cost allocation changes and those data do not show a systematic bias harming smaller zones.  Those data, in fact, show that the changes in zonal load change from year to year and that many smaller zones benefit from the elimination of the de minimis threshold.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and EKPC largely ignore competing evidence provided in the Neptune/LIPA Complaint proceeding that confirms the problematic effect that the         de minimis threshold has on cost allocation, including that all zones in the PJM region had usage below the de minimis threshold for 132 of 291 transmission facilities in 2022, suggesting that the assignment of cost responsibility is not based on usage.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners claim that this outcome “proves nothing by itself,” given that most projects are small and are unlikely to have impacts in other zones.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners ignore, however, evidence cited in the Order on Remand suggesting that for 18 projects the de minimis threshold excluded certain zones from being allocated any costs, notwithstanding the measured use attributed to those zones pursuant to the DFAX analysis.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ argument likewise does not confront the example of a transmission facility where 90.12% of the flows were exempt from payment due to the de minimis threshold resulting in the remaining zone being allocated 100% of the costs.  We are similarly not convinced by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ argument that the Commission failed to select a just and reasonable replacement rate due to the impact of reallocations.  By eliminating the de minimis threshold, the replacement rate ensures that costs will be allocated based on each zone’s use of the facility.  The fact that application of the replacement rate may result in reallocations to reflect a zone’s use of the facility does not render the replacement rate unjust and unreasonable.
We are likewise not convinced by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ suggestion that the Commission relied too heavily on “[a]dditional evidence provided in the [Neptune/LIPA] Complaint” from 2020 and the court’s opinion.  As discussed above, the court’s findings alone are sufficient to be dispositive.  Further, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners understate the evidence considered by the Commission.  In addition to evidence provided in the Neptune/LIPA Complaint, the Commission’s determination was supported by economic theory and consideration of record evidence put forth by other parties.  As such, the Commission acted well within its broad discretion in finding that the existing record was sufficient to make a determination. 
Effects of Alternative Proposals
Rehearing Request
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that the Commission failed to appropriately consider the impact of allocation changes created by the Settlement Proposal and Host Zone Proposal.  They claim that the Settlement Proposal addressed the basis of the D.C. Circuit’s concerns regarding the de minimis threshold by limiting the application of the 1% de minimis threshold and providing for integrated treatment of merchant exporters.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners suggest that under the Settlement Proposal merchant exporters would no longer be treated as smaller zones when applying the de minimis threshold.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners state that this resolves the D.C. Circuit’s concerns without eliminating the de minimis threshold altogether, an outcome which PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue would have the effect of substantially increasing costs for customers in “a number of” smaller zones.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners additionally state that the Commission ignored the impact the Settlement Proposal and Host Zone Proposal would have on the examples provided by Neptune/LIPA that the Commission relied on in the Order on Remand.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners point to the example of an upgrade discussed in the Order on Remand, in which the costs were 100% assigned to the PECO Energy (PECO) zone.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners claim that, under the Host Zone Proposal, 100% of the costs of the project would have instead been more logically allocated to the zones with the largest DFAX values, including to the host zone PSEG.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners suggest that the Commission erred by rejecting the Settlement Proposal’s remedy—which would correct the unjust outcome for the PECO zone cited as an example by the Commission in the Order on Remand—while instead adopting its own remedy that results in cost shifts and rate shocks.
Commission Determination
We are not convinced by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ arguments that the Commission failed to adequately consider the impact of adopting the Settlement Proposal and Host Zone Proposal.  
Neither proposal fully addresses the court’s concerns with the existing de minimis threshold.  Instead, the Host Zone Proposal revises the PJM Tariff to provide that the                      de minimis threshold will not apply to the zone in which the relevant transmission facility is located, but will continue to apply to other zones.  As a result, those other zones will be assigned costs that will, per the court’s concerns, be based on their “use of a facility relative to their total load” and, as such, would not be consistent with cost causation principles.  In addition to the Host Zone Proposal’s features, the Settlement Proposal would also integrate merchant transmission facilities into the zone in which they are connected for purposes of calculating cost assignments under the solution-based DFAX method.  Both the Host Zone Proposal and the Settlement Proposal would continue to exempt non-host zones even though those zones make use of the transmission facility and therefore do not address the court’s concerns and would be unjust and unreasonable.
We are not convinced by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ contention that the Settlement Proposal would resolve the D.C. Circuit’s concern that “the 1% de minimis threshold works to the detriment of exporting merchant zones.”  Even assuming PJM Indicated Transmission Owners are correct that the Settlement Proposal would remedy the treatment of merchant zones as separate PJM zones for purposes of calculating cost assignments under the solution-based DFAX method, the D.C. Circuit did not limit its concern to the impact of the de minimis threshold on merchant zones.  Rather, the court found that PJM’s use of the de minimis threshold based on the size of zones when benefits were measured according to MW usage of a transmission facility was unduly discriminatory.  The Settlement Proposal does not purport to cure this issue and, like the Host Zone Proposal, retains the existing de minimis threshold for some zones that the D.C. Circuit found to be unjust and unreasonable.  
We are not convinced by PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ argument that removing the use of de minimis threshold for host zones ensures a just and reasonable allocation of costs, noting that the Host Zone Proposal would mitigate concerns regarding a particular project discussed in the Order on Remand as an example of unreasonable outcomes.  Again assuming for the sake of argument that PJM Indicated Transmission Owners are correct that the Host Zone Proposal resolves some issues by allocating costs to the host zone, it is unsurprising that a proposal that partially eliminates the de minimis threshold (i.e., for host zones, but not other zones) improves outcomes to some extent.  This modification does not change the fact that the Host Zone Proposal, which retains the existing de minimis threshold for certain zones, could still distort the cost allocation for other zones.  Moreover, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ assertion that the Host Zone Proposal would result in a just and reasonable cost allocation for one project out of the hundreds that PJM selects every year does not demonstrate that that the continued use of the de minimis threshold in the Host Zone Proposal would not result in cost allocation distortions for other projects.  
Rationale for De Minimis Threshold
Rehearing Requests
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and EKPC claim that the Commission failed to consider the purpose of the de minimis threshold to “prevent the unjust and unreasonable allocation of transmission upgrade costs to customers in zones with minimal reliance on the transmission upgrades.”  According to PJM Indicated Transmission Owners, the threshold is meant to exclude low DFAX results that reflect minimal reliance by customers in a zone or a merchant transmission facility, and that may represent aberrational results.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners note the threshold was raised from 0.1% to 1% in 2012.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners suggest that, in eliminating the threshold, the Commission did not explain how it is just and reasonable to allocate RTEP upgrades costs to customers in zones with DFAX values so low that they reflect minimal reliance on the transmission upgrade at issue.
Commission Determination
In the Order on Remand, the Commission acknowledged PJM Indicated Transmission Owners’ contention that the de minimis threshold should be preserved to ensure that zones that make relatively insignificant use of a transmission facility are not allocated substantial costs.  We continue to find that the previous DFAX-based                 de minimis threshold did not properly capture a zone’s relative usage and benefits of transmission facilities, and thus violated the cost causation principle and was unjust and unreasonable.  Although we remain open to considering a modified version of the                de minimis threshold in the future, the modified de minimis thresholds in the alternative proposals submitted in this proceeding present the same concerns the court identified with the existing de minimis threshold.  Further, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners point to no authority for their suggestion that de minimis thresholds are necessary to allocate upgrade costs in a just and reasonable manner under PJM’s solution-based DFAX method.  Regardless, we find the risk of zones being allocated disproportionate costs once the de minimis threshold is removed to be low here.  Costs in PJM will continue to be assigned to the users of an upgrade based on their proportional usage.  Thus, costs will be allocated based on usage, without exemptions. 
Impact on Opinion No. 494 Settlement
Rehearing Request
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners allege that the Commission did not consider how the Order on Remand would impact the settlement previously approved in Docket No. EL05-121 (Opinion No. 494 Settlement), which addressed methods of assignment of cost responsibility for certain high-voltage transmission facilities within the PJM footprint.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners state that the Opinion No. 494 Settlement was the product of complex negotiations and contained “different methods for recovery of costs incurred for certain transmission upgrades.”  They claim that the parties to the settlement assumed the de minimis threshold would be an ongoing component of the cost allocation for projects.  They argue that the Commission did not consider that the refunds required by the Order on Remand would include a reallocation of costs that were assigned under the Opinion No. 494 Settlement, upsetting expectations.
Commission Determination
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners raise this argument for the first time on rehearing.  As discussed above, we do not consider arguments or new evidence raised for the first time on rehearing, subject to narrow exceptions.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners had the opportunity to raise this argument regarding a settlement filed in 2016 before the Order on Remand, but did not do so.  Accordingly, this argument is procedurally barred.  
Regardless, we are not persuaded that the outcome here would disrupt the parties’ expectations.  As PJM Indicated Transmission Owners acknowledge, the Opinion No. 494 Settlement was filed after the Con Edison Complaint.  As the application of the de minimis threshold was challenged in the Con Edison Complaint, all PJM Indicated Transmission Owners were on notice of the risk of the litigation-induced change from the date of the complaint.  More importantly, the Commission and the parties recognized that the Opinion No. 494 Settlement was subject to change based on the complaints:
We recognize that, more recently, the concerns raised by the contesting parties, are pending in complaint proceedings, regarding the justness and reasonableness of the hybrid cost allocation method for the 50% cost responsibility assigned pursuant to the solution-based DFAX method (at least in certain circumstances).  To the extent that the contesting parties were to prevail in those separate proceedings and the determination affects the Covered Transmission Enhancements in the Settlement, Section 2.2(c)(ii) of the Settlement provides that “nothing in this Settlement shall prevent the Commission from adjusting the Current Recovery Charges, as necessary, if the Commission modifies the charges that the owner(s) of a Covered Transmission Enhancement are authorized to recover.
Future consideration of de minimis threshold 
Clarification Request
Neptune/LIPA assert that they presented analyses of alternative MW usage-based thresholds at 0 MW, 5 MW, 10 MW, and 20 MW, but that the Commission did not address the potential merits of a MW usage-based de minimis threshold in the Order on Remand.  Neptune/LIPA seek clarification that the prior inclusion of a MW                   usage-based de minimis threshold as a part of a proposed remedy for the Neptune/LIPA Complaint does not preclude a future proposal of a prospective MW usage-based                  de minimis threshold for application within the DFAX cost allocation assignment procedure.  
Commission Determination
As stated in the Order on Remand, “we remain open to considering alternative             de minimis exemptions.”  We acknowledge that Neptune/LIPA previously recommended that the Commission direct a remedy by which PJM implements a uniform 20 MW usage de minimis threshold.  We clarify that nothing in the Order on Remand was intended to prejudge a future proposal including such an alternative threshold. 
Refunds 
Because the Commission directed elimination of the de minimis threshold as the just and reasonable replacement rate, the Commission found it appropriate in the Order on Remand to require PJM to correct its billing and provide relief to the parties.  Specifically, the Commission directed PJM, on behalf of the PJM transmission owners, to recalculate the cost allocations in Schedule 12 and correct the billing (with interest calculated pursuant to section 35.19(a) of the Commission’s regulations) for all projects subject to the solution-based DFAX cost allocation method back to June 18, 2015, the date on which the Commission committed legal error by denying Con Edison’s Complaint.
Refund Effective Date and Refund Period 
Rehearing Requests
On rehearing, parties generally challenge the Commission’s directive to recalculate cost responsibility assignments for the period beginning June 18, 2015.  Parties argue that pursuant to FPA section 206, the Commission may only issue refunds for a 15-month period.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners state that FPA section 206 provides a limited scope to the Commission’s refund authority, requiring the Commission to establish a refund effective date “whenever the Commission institutes a proceeding” under FPA section 206, with no exceptions.
The ICC requests clarification that the refunds and surcharges that the Commission ordered PJM to assess for the period beginning June 18, 2015 must be limited to a maximum of 15 months, pursuant to FPA section 206(b), and in the alternative seeks rehearing on this point.  The ICC argues that pursuant to FPA              section 206(b), the refund effective date cannot be established on the date of Commission error.
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that the Commission did not make the requisite finding in the initial 2015 order on the FPA section 206 complaints that the existing rate is unjust and unreasonable, and therefore, there is inadequate notice to justify the Commission’s order to pay refunds and surcharges.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners and the ICC argue that the Commission must establish a refund effective date as a prerequisite for issuing refunds under FPA section 206.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that the Commission did not publish a notice of refund effective date to mark the 15-month refund period provided under FPA                section 206(b) in the Con Edison and Linden Complaint proceedings and therefore no refunds can legally be required for the period prior to December 31, 2020, the date the Commission established as the refund effective date for the Neptune/LIPA Complaint.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. FERC, the D.C. Circuit expressly recognized that FPA section 206(b) “provides the relief FERC may order for amounts paid in excess of the just and reasonable rate[]” and that “refunds of any amounts paid outside the refund period are forbidden.”  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners further argue that the court stated that the Commission “cannot order utilities to give back money already collected (except for money collected during the limited refund period).”
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that the Commission did not direct PJM to recalculate any past billings and issue any refunds or surcharges to resettle those amounts pursuant to a 15-month refund period established under FPA section 206(b).  Instead, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that Ordering Paragraph (F) directs PJM to assess refunds and surcharges, including interest, from June 18, 2015 through          90 days from the date of the Order on Remand.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that the Commission cites no statutory authority, court, or regulatory precedent that authorizes the sweeping refund and surcharge obligations it seeks to impose on the PJM region, based on legal error or otherwise.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that remedial action under FPA section 309 “cannot be used to supersede specific statutory strictures” and as such, there is no basis for the Commission to have relied on this provision.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that the Commission did not invoke FPA section 309 in the Order on Remand, but even if it had, the Commission’s authority under FPA section 309 is limited to “clear, remedial action” consistent with the FPA.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners state that FPA section 309 provides no basis for the Commission to ignore the 15-month limitation set forth in FPA section 206(b).  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that even if the Commission is acting pursuant to its remedial authority in FPA section 309, it is limited to directing refunds for a single 15-month period, and that period begins on the December 31, 2020 refund effective date established in the Neptune/LIPA Complaint.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners claim that predictability “outweighs the value of being able to correct for decisions that in hindsight may appear unsound.”  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that the Commission’s interpretation “that it possesses infinite refund authority” would nullify the 15-month limitation Congress encoded in FPA section 206(b).
The ICC, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners, and PJM further contend that the Commission’s decision to institute surcharges is an unfair departure from Louisiana Public Service Commission v. FERC.  The ICC contends that in La. Pub. Serv. Comm’n the D.C. Circuit declined to issue refunds or make retroactive adjustments in a cost allocation case, stating that “[i]n a case where the company collected the proper level of revenues, but it is later determined that those revenues should have been allocated differently, the Commission traditionally has declined to order refunds.”  PJM argues that the Commission has moved away from its general policy of not requiring resettlements in cases of cost allocation or rate design, but asserts that this does not excuse the Commission from explaining how its decision to reallocate costs for the entire PJM region for costs approved 11 years ago is just and reasonable.
Commission Determination 
We sustain the Commission’s decision to require PJM to correct its billing and provide relief for all projects subject to the solution-based DFAX cost allocation method back to June 18, 2015.  The Commission directed remedies in this instance pursuant to its FPA section 309 authority to correct legal error.  We therefore do not agree with arguments that the Commission’s refund authority in this proceeding was limited to the 15-month period provided in FPA section 206.    
We disagree that the Commission cannot rely on FPA section 309 to direct refunds because it did not expressly invoke this authority in the Order on Remand.  FPA section 309 provides the Commission the “power to perform any and all acts ... as it may find necessary or appropriate to carry out the provisions of” the FPA.  The D.C. Circuit has held that the Commission’s remedial authority is “expansive” and “permits [the Commission] to advance remedies not expressly provided by the FPA, as long as they are consistent with the Act.”  The Commission does not need to expressly “reserve” its section 309 authority to use it.  
Recently, the D.C. Circuit confronted a similar question regarding the Commission’s ability to direct refunds to remedy legal error.  MISO Transmission Owners II involved a prolonged dispute over the return-on-equity (ROE) rate component paid to transmission owners in the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) region.  In 2013, electric customers filed complaints with the Commission alleging that MISO transmission owners’ ROE of 12.38% was unjust and unreasonable under the FPA.  In its initial series of orders, the Commission addressed the complaints and concluded that the ROE was unjust and unreasonable and directed refunds for the 15-month refund period from the date of the initial complaint.  In MISO Transmission Owners I, the D.C. Circuit vacated and remanded that initial series of orders back to the Commission.  In MISO Transmission Owners II, the D.C. Circuit reviewed the Commission’s subsequent orders on remand, and found that, in addition to properly ordering refunds for the 15-month refund period under FPA section 206, the Commission had also properly directed refunds to be effective September 28, 2016, the date of the Commission’s initial order.  In considering whether the Commission could issue retroactive refunds, the court analyzed whether the “[Commission] relied on its authority under section 309 in a way that appears inconsistent with the refund limitations imposed by section 206.”  The D.C. Circuit concluded that the Commission’s actions were consistent with its statutory mandate, explaining the Commission is not limited to the 15-month refund period as articulated in FPA section 206 and may rely on FPA section 309 in remedying legal error.  The D.C. Circuit reasoned that the petitioners “are generally correct” that section 206(b) limits refunds to 15 months.  But the court stated that:
However, there is a clear exception in play in this case.  Where, as here, FERC is “remedy[ing] its own errors after being reversed in court[,] ... ‘[t]his court has ... recognized FERC’s authority to order retroactive rate adjustments.’” … This authority is based in part on the concept that when FERC sets a new rate that is subject to further review, the relevant stakeholders are “aware in advance of the risk of                   litigation-induced change” and thus on notice that “judicial invalidation of Commission decisions [could] result[ ] in retroactive changes in rates.”  
Similarly, the Commission in this proceeding is acting to correct legal error identified by the D.C. Circuit in remanding and vacating the Commission’s orders upholding the use of the de minimis threshold.    
On rehearing, PJM argues that because this proceeding involves cost allocation, not cost recovery, refunds are not appropriate.  We disagree.  As La. Pub. Serv. Comm’n states, the Commission does not have a general policy concerning refunds in cost allocation and rate design cases.  Rather, “the Commission will consider whether to require refunds in cost allocation and rate design cases based on the specific facts and equities of each case, even where such refunds must be funded through surcharges on certain parties.”  Here, the Commission found that the circumstances presented in this case warrant refunds.  In particular, the entities that initiated these proceedings are entitled to refunds for the period in which they paid higher rates due to application of the de minimis threshold.  When the Commission commits legal error, there is a strong presumption that the proper remedy is to return the parties to the positions they would have been but for the Commission’s error.  Moreover, as discussed below, every case involving refunds necessarily implicates some level of reliance interests, but that does not categorically bar refunds.
Filed Rate Doctrine/Retroactive Rulemaking
Rehearing Request 
Rehearing parties contend that the Commission’s directive for PJM to issue refunds and surcharges for all PJM RTEP projects subject to the solution-based DFAX cost allocation method effective June 2015 constitutes impermissible retroactive ratemaking and violates the filed rate doctrine.  
The ICC contends that courts and regulated entities are prohibited from retroactively changing filed rates and the Commission has no authority to alter a rate retroactively.  The ICC argues that the filed rate doctrine “binds regulated entities to charge only the rates filed with FERC and to change their rates only prospectively.”  The ICC further contends that the filed rate doctrine is not limited to rates, but also extends to cost allocation, the elimination of the de minimis threshold and the replacement rate.  The ICC argues that the Commission cannot rely upon FPA            section 206(b) to institute refunds on a retroactive basis.    
The ICC argues that the Commission’s direction to PJM to retroactively reallocate and impose rate increases is not exempt from the prohibition on retroactive rate increases.  The ICC cites Verso for the proposition that the Commission lacks the authority under FPA section 206(b) to grant retroactive refunds and surcharges.  The ICC attempts to distinguish Verso, which ultimately permitted a retroactive cost reallocation, on the premise that there, the Commission determined a refund effective date, whereas here, there was no refund effective date directed in the complaint orders. 
Additionally, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that without setting the refund effective date, the Commission lacks the authority to direct retroactive refunds.  The ICC argues that section 206(b) is a narrow exception to the filed rate doctrine’s general prohibition on retroactive rate modifications, but when warranted, it directs the Commission to establish a refund effective date upon the commencement of the              section 206 proceeding to award the refunds and that the Commission failed to do so here.    
Both the ICC and PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that the notice exception to the filed rate doctrine, applicable in certain circumstances where ratepayers have had sufficient notice that an approved rate is subject to change, is only satisfied when entities have a formal notice through a Commission proceeding or the courts that a rate may change.  The ICC contends that notice is inapplicable in this circumstance because the generators in PJM’s transmission zones subject to the de minimis threshold had no notice that the Commission might reallocate all transmission project costs from over 11 years ago.  Similarly, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that customers had no notice of the broad resettlement requirement given the limited parties, time periods, and claims involved in the underlying litigation.
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that even if the complaints themselves constitute notice that some cost allocations would change, that notice would only extend to the allocations directly challenged by Con Edison and Linden insofar as they impacted Con Edison and merchant transmission exporters.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that not all the customers in PJM paying refunds were on notice that they would be subject to refunds and surcharges as a result of the Con Edison and Linden Complaint proceedings for all projects, beyond those associated with specific projects, time periods and parties.  Moreover, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that the 11-year refund liability covering hundreds of projects in PJM will result in billions of dollars of surcharges being extracted from customers who had no way of knowing that they may face a potential PJM-wide retroactive resettlement and refund obligation.  
Similarly, PJM argues that while all customers were on notice that the              solution-based DFAX method’s de minimis threshold might change, the nature and scope of the effects was uncertain.  Indeed, PJM argues that given the effects of removing the de minimis threshold from the allocations, which is a highly technical evaluation involving models, tools, and data with complex calculations, it is infeasible that ratepayers surcharged in the past for under-allocations would fully understand their potential liability starting in 2015.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners similarly contend that the Commission’s refund directive will impose refund liability on some customers that could not have had any knowledge or reasonable expectation that those purchases and the myriad transactions that turned on those purchases would be upended by a Commission order on three complaints filed by entities exporting power from PJM.  
Commission Determination
We do not agree that the Commission’s directive for PJM to issue refunds and surcharges violates the filed rate doctrine or its corollary, the prohibition against retroactive ratemaking.  Having determined that the Commission committed legal error, the Commission properly considered whether refunds were appropriate and, given the circumstances of this proceeding, found that they were.  In Xcel, the D.C. Circuit found that the Commission acted arbitrarily when it did not weigh the equities of an energy utility’s request for retroactive refunds.  The D.C. Circuit found that the Commission’s position that “its section 205 error of law is irremediable beyond prospective relief” was “irreconcilable with the authority Congress granted it in section 309 to remedy its errors.”  More recently, in MISO Transmission Owners II, the D.C. Circuit affirmed this position, finding that in “situations when section 206 and section 309 may be in tension” the Commission acted reasonably when it “backdated the effective date of the relief ordered …. pursuant to its remedial authority under FPA section 309” to remedy legal error.  
Contrary to the ICC’s arguments, nothing in Verso constrains the Commission’s ability to act in this proceeding.  Both MISO Transmission Owners II and Verso recite the standard limitation on retroactive refunds under FPA section 206(b).  And like MISO Transmission Owners II, albeit in different factual circumstances, Verso also affirmed the Commission’s reliance on FPA section 309 as providing the Commission with expansive remedial authority to advance remedies not expressly provided by the FPA, as long as they are consistent with the FPA.  Ultimately, the Verso court found that the reallocation of past costs, including through surcharges, was “well within” the Commission’s remedial authority under section 309, read in harmony with section 206.  On rehearing, the ICC contends that Verso is not controlling in this instance because in that proceeding the Commission established a refund effective date under FPA             section 206(b), whereas here, the Commission’s complaint orders did not set a refund effective date.  However, the court’s decision in Verso did not turn on the establishment of a refund effective date.  Moreover, here the Commission’s authority to direct refunds back to September 1, 2015, is based on the finding that the Commission engaged in legal error, regardless of whether a refund effective date was set.  In other words, the Commission’s authority here allows it to do now, on remand from the court, what it could have done had it not committed legal error in the complaint orders: provide for refunds back to the date on which the Commission committed legal error.
Further, we find that the complaint proceedings provided adequate notice of the potential for resettlements.  The Commission has previously found that complaints provide “notice of the possibility that the challenged rate will change.”  The D.C. Circuit affirmed this position in MISO Transmission Owners II, stating that “stakeholders are ‘aware in advance of the risk of litigation induced change’ and thus on notice that ‘judicial invalidation of Commission decisions [could] result[] in retroactive changes in rates.’”  Because the de minimis threshold was challenged in the Con Edison Complaint as unjust and unreasonable, all parties were on notice as of the date of the Commission’s order denying the complaint that there was a risk of litigation-induced change and that the potential judicial invalidation of the Commission’s decision could result in retroactive changes in rates.  
Surcharge
Rehearing Request 
The ICC argues that the Commission lacks the authority under the FPA and Commission precedent to require surcharges to recover an underpayment due to the Commission’s legal error.  The ICC argues that FPA section 206(b) does not permit surcharges to address rates that were too low, although it authorizes refunds to address rates that were too high in certain circumstances.
PJM argues that requiring surcharges is unfair where the extent of the change in allocations from removing the de minimis threshold is uncertain and the parties that will be surcharged have no way of knowing the extent of their potential liability. 
Commission Determination 
We are unpersuaded by the arguments on rehearing that the Commission cannot require surcharges to recover an underpayment due to the Commission’s legal error.  The Commission has the authority to implement surcharges to remedy legal error. 
First, the ICC’s assertion that surcharges are not permissible to implement a remedy warranted to correct legal error is inaccurate.  The ICC cites Verso, where the D.C. Circuit stated that the Commission has “no concomitant authority … to retroactively correct rates that were too low” in support of this assertion.  But the D.C. Circuit made this statement in the context of discussing the Commission’s FPA section 206(b) authority, not the Commission’s FPA section 309 authority.  To the contrary, the Verso court expressly stated that the Commission “had authority to order refunds and corresponding surcharges under Section 206 and its broad remedial authority under Section 309.”  As in Verso, here surcharges are required to carry out the directed refunds.  Because PJM is a revenue-neutral organization, such that it must receive payments from market participants in order to distribute the refunds to relevant market participants, resettlements required to eliminate the de minimis threshold can only be accomplished via surcharges.  Given that the Commission directed PJM to implement surcharges to remedy the legal error under its FPA section 309 authority, we find this action is consistent with the Commission’s statutory authority and relevant precedent.  
Correcting Legal Error
Rehearing Requests
On rehearing, parties contend that the Commission is unable to direct the extent of refunds and surcharges as directed in the Order on Remand solely on the basis of correcting legal error.
PJM contends that while the Commission may have the authority under FPA sections 206 and 309 to institute surcharges and refunds, it failed to invoke any statutory or precedential authority to direct resettlements or surcharges in the Order on Remand.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that the Commission cannot impose over one billion dollars in refund liability on PJM customers justified only upon the legal error doctrine.  
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that even if the Commission has authority to direct refunds beyond the 15-month period, that authority is limited to remedying the specific error at issue.  PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that the Remand Opinion did not require the Commission to eliminate the 1% de minimis threshold in its entirety, and therefore the Commission’s decision to eliminate the 1%           de minimis threshold went beyond correcting the legal error identified by the D.C. Circuit.  Similarly, the ICC contends that although the D.C. Circuit invalidated the            de minimis threshold, the court did not direct or require the retroactive reallocation of all project costs for 11-plus years – it contends that this decision was made by the Commission.
