PJM Indicated Transmission Owners argue that even if the Commission had the authority to order refunds to correct its legal error, the scope of the refunds must be confined to putting the “parties in the position they would have been in had the error not been made.”
PJM Indicated Transmission Owners contend that in the ConEd and Linden Complaint proceedings and the Neptune/LIPA proceedings, the Commission erred by failing to consider how the de minimis threshold affects merchant transmission exporters in an unduly discriminatory manner but this legal error does not provide it with unfettered refund authority to apply its finding across PJM.
Commission Determination
We disagree that the Commission’s authority to remedy its legal error in this proceeding bars the remedy directed in the Order on Remand.  As an initial matter, as discussed above, the Commission has latitude in developing its remedy, and has the authority to issue refunds pursuant to its FPA section 309 remedial authority.  Here, the Commission has not directed or assumed “unfettered” refund authority, but instead, is reasonably ensuring that PJM customers are restored to the position in which they would have been if the Commission’s legal error had not occurred.
Next, we find arguments that the D.C. Circuit did not require the Commission to eliminate the de minimis threshold, and thus the Commission’s determination to eliminate the de minimis threshold and direct refunds to miss the mark.  Here, the D.C. Circuit expressly found that the Commission erred in upholding PJM’s de minimis threshold as just and reasonable and remanded the proceeding.  The D.C. Circuit further found that “[b]ecause the de minimis threshold regularly produces ‘wholesale departure[s] from the cost-causation principle,’ it cannot be considered just and reasonable.”  PJM and PJM Indicated Transmission Owners do not dispute that the de minimis threshold applied to transmission projects selected in the RTEP subject to the solution-based DFAX cost allocation method.  Thus, given that the court’s reasoning, like the Commission’s in the Order on Remand, is not limited to the application of the threshold to any particular project identified in the complaint, the Commission reasonably exercised its discretion in adopting a remedy that corrects its error in previously upholding the threshold.
As the court stated in MISO Transmission Owners, “[t]he relevant inquiry … is whether FERC’s ultimate remedy appropriately cures the errors identified by this court.”  Here, the Commission’s directed refunds are an appropriate remedy to the legal error of upholding the de minimis threshold, for all transmission projects selected through the RTEP that are subject to the solution-based DFAX cost allocation method.  Contrary to rehearing parties’ arguments, the directed relief is narrowly tailored to the specific error of upholding the de minimis threshold and calculating corresponding refunds and surcharges from the date of the Commission’s legal error.  Thus, the Commission’s elimination of the de minimis threshold and the requirement to pay refunds and surcharges is reasonable and not an “unfettered” application of authority.

Commission Determination
On rehearing, PJM contends that refunds and surcharges will be too complicated, requiring substantial time and effort to modify software to re-run models/simulations and ultimately finalize the updated cost responsibility assignments, and therefore the Commission should exercise its discretion to not institute refunds.  
While the Commission’s remedial authority is discretionary, it must be grounded in consideration of equitable factors.  Here, however, the equities weigh in favor of directing refunds.  Consistent with the court’s conclusions in the Remand Opinion, the Commission has found that the de minimis threshold challenged in the complaint proceeding results in assignments of cost responsibility that are unjust and unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.  As discussed earlier, in weighing the equities the Commission must consider the fact that, without refunds, the New York parties that initiated these proceedings would receive no reimbursement for their overpayments resulting from the use of the de minimis threshold and three of the            New York parties would not receive any benefit from prospective application because they are no longer subject to cost allocation under the PJM tariff.  More generally, as explained above, neither the court’s nor the Commission’s reasoning in finding the             de minimis threshold unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory is limited to the application of that threshold to particular projects; the threshold is part of the RTEP cost allocation method applicable to all transmission projects in PJM that are subject to the solution-based DFAX cost allocation method.  In these circumstances, limiting refunds to only complaining parties for remedying legal error that is generally applicable to all may not be reasonable.  Regarding the duration of the refund period, we find that it is appropriately tailored to remedy the legal error, which occurred on June 18, 2015.  In addition, failure to institute refunds in this proceeding could incentivize public utilities and other entities to prolong the appellate process in future proceedings in hopes that they would not have to repay the over-paid sums.  Thus, in balancing these equities here, we find that the equities favor the payment of refunds and the imposition of surcharges. 
Rehearing parties further allege that the Commission has previously weighed the equities and ultimately denied refunds in prior Commission proceedings.  Yet, most of the proceedings which parties rely upon to support their arguments do not involve remedies for a legal error, as presented here.  In cases involving the Commission’s legal error, there is a strong presumption that the proper remedy is to return the stakeholders to the positions they would have been but for the Commission’s error.  When weighing the equities, this presumption weighs in favor of granting a remedy.     
The one instance PJM cited where the Commission addressed a circumstance involving legal error and declined to institute refunds, the Minimum Offer Price Rule Remand Order, is distinguishable.  In that proceeding, the D.C. Circuit found that the Commission exceeded its authority under FPA section 205 when it accepted, subject to condition, PJM’s proposal introducing two new categorical exemptions from the Minimum Offer Price Rule, and extending the mitigation period from one to three years.  On remand, the Commission rejected the filing in its entirety and declined to direct refunds for the period between the effective date of PJM’s initial filing in 2012 and the date of the order on remand in 2017.  There, the Commission found that issuing refunds for this period would require PJM to rerun the market under PJM’s pre-existing tariff in 2012 which would cause significant disruptions (such as harm to customers), could result in either duplicative commitments or lost commitments for certain resources, and also presented capital and regulatory risk.  However, the Commission noted that “the legal error in this case involves the Commission’s improper revision of PJM’s filing under FPA section 205, not the merits of the competitive entry and self-supply exemptions that were implemented during the relevant period and which the Commission found just and reasonable.”  Thus, the Commission concluded that “leaving the auction results undisturbed is therefore consonant with the underlying purpose of the [Minimum Offer Price Rule] in that competitive resources were not subject to the offer floor under the market design in effect during the relevant timeframe.”  The Commission further found that the offers in the MOPR proceeding were competitive offers and therefore rerunning the auction would result in prices higher than competition warranted.  In contrast here, there is no auction, and both the court and the Commission have concluded that the de minimis threshold fails on its “merits,” i.e., it is unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory.  Accordingly, the Commission’s selected remedy addresses that specific error by removing the de minimis threshold and refunding the amounts paid back to the date of the Commission’s legal error, June 18, 2015.    
While rehearing parties allege that here, they similarly made business decisions based upon the de minimis threshold, we find the analogy unavailing.  Reliance interests are present to some degree in every case involving refunds, yet that fact does not categorically bar refunds—particularly when the Commission is remedying a legal error under FPA section 309.  In other words, reliance is one of the equitable factors that the Commission must weigh in determining whether to order refunds, but is not dispositive.  Rehearing parties also were on notice from the complaint and appeal that refunds and surcharges might ultimately be directed.  
Rehearing parties raise additional equitable concerns in support of denying refunds, such as to the difficulty of fully calculating and shifting amounts to entities that were over-allocated costs, rate shock, creditworthiness, and whether the entities entitled to or required to pay refunds will be the same as the entities that over- or  underpaid as a result of the de minimis threshold.  Such arguments are premature at this time, given that we are setting issues regarding the calculation method for refunds and surcharges raised in PJM’s request for clarification for hearing and settlement judge procedures, in order to determine a reasonable method of determining refunds and surcharges.  While we are requiring PJM to issue refunds dating back to June 18, 2015, the time of legal error, the hearing and settlement judge will contemplate the structure of such refunds, and the timing for PJM to make these resettlements has not yet been set.  Thus, some of the impacts of refunds may be mitigated in the determination of how refunds are processed, and we therefore find that arguments pertaining to the calculation, billing impacts, and creditworthiness of entities are not yet ripe for review.  
Netting	
In the Remand Opinion, the D.C. Circuit held that the Commission reasonably explained its decision to uphold netting under the solution-based DFAX method because “it produces a different benefit by creating extra capacity for the transmission line.”  The D.C. Circuit noted that negative flows make additional capacity available because power flows in opposite directions offset each other, decreasing the amount of power flowing over the line as compared to zones with flows in only one direction.  The          D.C. Circuit stated that the Commission reasonably concluded that because counterflows offset flows in the opposite direction the Commission “could reasonably treat them as benefits that the zones confer on the facility, rather than benefits that they derive from it.”  As such, the court held, “counterflows can reasonably be considered a basis for discounting rather than increasing a zone’s cost allocation.”
The D.C. Circuit noted that the approach approved by the Commission was not necessarily the only reasonable one.  The D.C. Circuit also recognized that the Commission had ordered further proceedings to consider netting in response to the Neptune/LIPA Complaint, which had been filed after the Commission issued the orders under review on appeal.  The D.C. Circuit held that, while the Commission reasonably explained its decision to approve netting in the proceedings under appeal, the court was not prejudging the Neptune/LIPA Complaint and did not foreclose the Commission from reconsidering its position on netting based on the evidence and arguments in that proceeding.
In the Order on Remand, the Commission denied Neptune/LIPA’s Complaint in Docket No. EL21-39-000 with respect to the netting provisions of the solution-based DFAX method, finding that Neptune/LIPA raised arguments it considered when denying the Con Edison and Linden Complaints.  In particular, the Commission continued to find “that accounting for counter-flow in zonal netting is an important factor in considering a load’s contribution to a particular constraint because it reduces the need for expanding that constraint” and “that netting appropriately accounts for the actual flow contribution from a zone using PJM generation to serve its own load which is consistent with the zonal nature of cost allocation.”  The Commission found that Neptune/LIPA had not met their FPA section 206 burden to demonstrate that PJM’s use of netting is an unjust and unreasonable methodology for calculating a zone’s use of the facility, and thus upheld PJM’s use of the current netting procedure in calculating solution-based DFAX cost allocation assignments.
Rehearing Request
On rehearing, Neptune/LIPA argue that the Commission failed to adequately consider new record evidence in upholding the use of the netting procedure.  First, Neptune/LIPA challenge the Commission’s finding that they raised the same arguments addressed in the Con Edison and Linden Complaint proceedings, instead contending that they submitted extensive new technical analyses and expert testimony demonstrating that the current netting procedure masks the modeled level of a zone’s usage of an upgrade, which distorts the DFAX calculations and cost allocation assignments.  Neptune/LIPA argue that netting undercounts usage benefits and causes improper and unjustified              cost-shifting between zones.
Neptune/LIPA argue that they documented how the assumption that netting accounts for zonal level benefits is fundamentally flawed because the solution-based DFAX analysis does not demonstrate that a zone’s directional positive and negative flows will occur simultaneously throughout the year.  Further Neptune/LIPA assert they explained that, to effectively identify beneficiaries of a transmission upgrade, PJM “must keep track of MW usage in both directions (i.e., nodally, without netting) to align with the tracking of MW-hours flow under the PJM production cost model.  PJM’s implementation of the current netting procedure within a Zonal DFAX calculation does not meet that fundamental test.”  
Neptune/LIPA contend the current netting procedure distorts cost allocation assignments by removing significant MW usage from cost allocation.  Neptune/LIPA cite their expert testimony, which stated that “[s]ince ‘netting’ produces a lower netted DFAX in a single direction, it is possible for a significant amount of MW usage in the same direction as the predominant flows demonstrated in the 8,760 hours production cost simulation [to be] entirely removed from the cost-allocation process.”  Neptune/LIPA contend that this conclusion demonstrates that netting “removes a significant amount of calculated usage from the cost-allocation process.”  
Neptune/LIPA argue that the host zones and adjacent zones derive benefits through MW usage in both the positive and negative direction, but that PJM’s current netting procedure undercounts usage benefits.  Neptune/LIPA also contend that the Commission did not support its finding that the netting procedure is not driving significant, anomalous, unjust and unreasonable cost allocation assignments and does not rely on the new evidence provided by Neptune/LIPA.
Next, Neptune/LIPA argue that the Commission improperly assumes that the netting procedure “is an important factor in considering a load’s contribution to a particular constraint because it reduces the need for expanding that constraint.”  Neptune/LIPA argue that this assumption is incorrect because the solution-based DFAX method measures a zone’s MW usage of the upgrade—not its contribution to an identified constraint or reduction of need thereto.  Moreover, Neptune/LIPA argue that the Commission’s finding that the netting procedure “accounts for the actual flow contribution from a zone for purpose of a zonal cost allocation” was in error because the Commission relied on a record that equates “contribution” to MW usage.  Neptune/LIPA argue that neither the solution-based DFAX method nor the current netting procedure identifies or quantifies cost allocation based on reduction of a constraint.  
Neptune/LIPA disagree with the Commission’s finding in the Order on Remand that netting accounts for counterflows.  Neptune/LIPA contend that the record illustrates that PJM accounts for counterflows through its 8,760 hours production cost analysis—not through the current netting procedure. 
Finally, Neptune/LIPA contend that the record shows that netting produces unjust and unreasonable cost allocations.  Specifically, Neptune/LIPA argue that:                  (1) solution-based DFAX method cost allocation results, after the current netting procedure is implemented, are wholly contrary to prevailing flows on the upgrade as determined by PJM’s 8,760 hours production cost analysis; (2) there are repeated        “jump-shifts” in the resulting cost allocations, null set outcomes and other anomalous outcomes directly caused by PJM’s implementation of the current netting procedures;        (3) the netting procedure produces anomalous results and removes significant MW usage across the PJM footprint (as evidenced through an analysis of 291 RTEP upgrade cost allocation assignments under an isolation scenario of the current netting procedure, without the de minimis threshold, showing the removal of 41.3% of the calculated MW usage in the positive direction and removal of 55.6% of the calculated MW usage in the negative direction).
Commission Determination
We continue to find that Neptune/LIPA have not demonstrated that the netting process in Schedule 12 is unjust and unreasonable.  While there may be other methods of calculating a zone’s net contribution to the use of a facility, Neptune/LIPA challenge PJM’s netting practice in the context of an FPA section 206 complaint, and the Commission therefore assessed whether PJM’s current netting process is just and reasonable; in a complaint proceeding the Commission’s analysis is not an exercise of determining whether there is another process that is just and reasonable or more just and reasonable than the current process.  
Under the solution-based DFAX method, PJM models the transfer of the net of energy flow in the positive and negative directions from generation to all load within a transmission zone during peak load conditions and models the transfer on a zonal basis, not on a bus-by-bus basis.  PJM’s current netting practice within the solution-based DFAX method reflects the zone’s overall use of the transmission project during peak load conditions.  This practice is just and reasonable because it appropriately reflects the fact that a zone’s bus-level power flows in opposite directions will offset each other and result in a combined zonal power flow.  Because power flow is modeled on a zonal basis, the cost allocation similarly reflects costs based upon the zone’s overall power flow.  Therefore, we continue to find PJM’s netting practice and corresponding cost allocation is just and reasonable.  
On rehearing, Neptune/LIPA contend that the PJM’s netting practice under the solution-based DFAX calculation removes “significant MW usage” and is therefore unjust and unreasonable.  But PJM’s calculation does not remove MW usage as Neptune/LIPA contend; instead, it accounts for the actual power flows given that the negative and positive flows offset each other.  We continue to find that this is a reasonable method because it measures the actual usage of the facility within the zone.  As discussed below, this metric accurately assesses constraints in the zone.  Neptune/LIPA’s arguments regarding the removal of usage suggest only that another calculation method would yield different results; they do not demonstrate that the current calculation is unjust and unreasonable.  Thus, Neptune/LIPA’s arguments do not satisfy their burden of proof on this point. 
Further, Neptune/LIPA’s arguments misconstrue the Commission’s findings in the Order on Remand.  On rehearing, Neptune/LIPA state that the Commission erred in relying on the findings from the Linden Complaint Order that netting was just and reasonable on the basis that “accounting for counter-flow in zonal netting is an important factor in considering a load’s contribution to a particular constraint because it reduces the need for expanding that constraint.”  Neptune/LIPA claim that this statement is incorrect because the solution-based DFAX method does not measure contribution of load to an identified constraint or reduction of need.  The costs of RTEP reliability projects, which are developed with the intention of reducing constraints, are allocated pursuant to PJM’s Tariff using the solution-based DFAX method.  While we agree that the solution-based DFAX method does not measure the contribution of load to the constraint, it does measure the benefit that the zone receives from relieving that constraint.  In using the solution-based DFAX method to calculate this benefit, netting of flows in each direction is a reasonable method of determining a zone’s actual flow on the facility during peak load conditions, and the corresponding benefit from relief of a constraint.  Because PJM’s RTEP process prospectively identifies reliability issues of its transmission system for the future and selects transmission projects to address the identified constraints or need, a zone’s net use of the facility is a reasonable measure of the benefit the zone derives from that facility.  Thus, we are not persuaded by arguments that the Commission improperly relied on the netting procedure in finding the             solution-based DFAX method just and reasonable.  
 Neptune/LIPA also contend that the Commission’s finding that PJM’s netting procedure “accounts for the actual flow contribution from a zone for purpose of a zonal cost allocation” is inaccurate.  They further argue “neither the Solution-Based DFAX methodology nor the current netting procedure identifies, much less quantifies, cost allocation based on reduction of a constraint need.”  However, as the D.C. Circuit found, “because counterflows increase capacity, FERC could reasonably treat them as benefits that the zones confer on the facility, rather than benefits that they derive from it.  So understood, counterflows can reasonably be considered a basis for discounting rather than increasing a zone’s cost allocation.”  In other words, a cost allocation method involving netting positive energy flows with negative counterflows is a just and reasonable method of determining cost allocation because it appropriately accounts for the fact that counterflows reduce the amount of additional transmission capacity needed to mitigate the constraint, which can reduce the cost of the facility being constructed.
Next, Neptune/LIPA argue the Commission erred in stating that netting accounts for counterflows.  They argue that the record instead establishes that PJM accounts for counterflows through its 8,760 hours production cost analysis, and not netting.  This is inaccurate; counterflows are used in both scenarios.  First, as Neptune/LIPA acknowledge, counterflows are used in the 8,760 hours analysis, to determine the total energy use of the relevant project by all zones in each direction over the course of a year, effectively determining the proportion of the cost of the facility attributable to use in one direction versus the other.  But, counterflows are also used in PJM’s Schedule 12 netting process.  Under the solution-based DFAX method, zones with a net DFAX in a given direction for the peak load model after accounting for counterflows pay a proportionate share of costs allocated to that direction.  Counterflows are thus used in different ways but have the same functional consequence: they offset positive flows, reduce the net load on a transmission facility, and thereby increase the available capacity of that facility.  
We find Neptune/LIPA’s further arguments that netting within the solution-based DFAX method produces unjust and unreasonable results unpersuasive.  First, we disagree that the results of the solution-based DFAX cost allocation, including the netting procedure, are inconsistent with the 8,760 hours production cost analysis.  Rather, the two are simply different and complementary methods for analyzing the use of a particular transmission facility.  The production cost model recognizes that a transmission facility supports net flows in both directions over the course of the year, and focuses on net flows for each hour over the course of the year to determine the portion of the time that the facility supports net flows in each direction.  The production model calculates flows in each direction independently, but for each hour it only calculates flows in one direction – the direction of net flow.  In contrast, the solution-based DFAX method determines the degree to which a zone relies on a particular project, and thereby benefits from the use of that project, under peak load conditions, as well as the direction of the zone’s net flow.  The amount and direction of net flow recognizes the degree to which the facility supports the zone’s flow contribution.  Thus, unsurprisingly, different analyses comparing different time periods will yield different results.  Similarly, the “jump-shifts” and analysis of the 291 RTEP upgrade cost allocations cited by Neptune/LIPA are all comparative analyses; they compare the result of netting under the solution-based DFAX method with an alternative calculation method.  These arguments do not demonstrate that PJM’s netting procedure is unjust and unreasonable; they demonstrate that a different method will produce different results, which does not satisfy Neptune/LIPA’s burden of proof.  We dismiss Neptune/LIPA’s arguments involving alternative measurements of calculating power flow.  Having found that PJM’s approach is not unjust and unreasonable, the Commission need not consider alternative methods of calculating a zone’s net contribution to the use of a project. 
Additional Arguments
Interest on Refunds 
Rehearing Request
PJM argues that if the Commission requires refunds, it should exercise its equitable discretion to waive the requirement of including interest.  PJM argues that the Commission failed to explain why interest is warranted under the facts of this case.  PJM states that while the Order on Remand was silent on the factors supporting interest, the Commission should perform a broader analysis on rehearing; and by doing so, it would recognize that the equities disfavor interest as a component of the resettlement.  PJM contends the Commission must properly evaluate whether interest is appropriate here.
PJM argues that the Commission has previously granted waiver of interest in similar cases involving legal error.  PJM states that granting interest in this case will be excessively broad and complex.  PJM contends that all customers throughout the PJM region are likely to be affected by reallocating the costs of over 1,200 projects, and therefore the resettlement ordered in this proceeding will not be as straightforward as in other cases.  PJM argues that because these calculations must be made manually, requiring interest will compound the adverse effects of the remedy, exacerbate the risk of error, and potentially lead to further litigation.  PJM further argues that the burden of these interest payments will fall on ordinary ratepayers who likely did not have notice for a case as long and complex as this one, and are unlikely to understand why they are being surcharged.  PJM contends that the Commission has previously denied interest in cases when parties were not on notice as to the “amount” of a future cost.
Alternatively, PJM requests that the Commission:  (1) use a lower interest rate that applies uniformly for the nearly 11 years relevant for refunds, rather than the rate calculated under 18 C.F.R. § 35.19a, which changes quarterly, and (2) direct PJM to calculate interest based on an alternative process than the orderly process proposed in its pleading.
Commission Determination
We sustain the result.  The Commission’s general policy is to require interest on refunds to ensure that the injured party is given the time-value of money.  Interest is simply a way of ensuring full compensation.  The Commission has previously stated that:
It is “the general rule” of the Commission that “a customer entitled to a refund should also be awarded interest in order to make it whole.”  The purpose of ordering interest paid is so that the recipient can be made whole for the time value of money that it otherwise would have available for its use. . . . In cases where full refunds are required, both the Commission and the courts have consistently treated interest as a necessary element of those refunds . . . . Interest, which merely represents use of the money, is ordinarily part of the refund of any overcharge, absent compelling reasons for not requiring its payment to the injured party.
This policy is applicable in instances when the Commission is remedying legal error.  While PJM points out the difficulties in determining the correct allocation of costs back to 2015 (which we are setting for hearing and settlement judge procedures), it has not explained why once those amounts are determined, it would be difficult to calculate interest in accordance with the Commission’s regulations.
PJM argues that, in other cases, the Commission has permitted parties to receive refunds with no interest.  However, the cases PJM cites in support of this assertion are not persuasive.  Panhandle, Trunkline, and Transco all involved separate determinations by the Commission regarding the pipeline’s ability to retroactively bill customers to recover production-related costs, as permitted in Order No. 94.  In each case, the Commission determined that it was unable to determine which party was injured, so the Commission awarded half of the disputed amount to each party.  On appeal, the D.C. Circuit affirmed the Commission’s remedy.  Notably, in affirming the Commission, the D.C. Circuit found that its determination was not a departure “from [the Commission’s] own general rule—that a customer entitled to a refund should also be awarded interest.”  This is because the Commission factored in what would have been considered interest in equitably resolving the disputed sums.  Thus, we do not find the cases cited by PJM to persuade us that refunds should not be issued with interest. 
Although we continue to find that refunds should be granted with interest, we note that the calculation of refunds to which this interest will apply is being set for hearing and settlement judge procedures.  
Updates to Historical Tariff Records
Rehearing Request 
PJM requests that the Commission exercise its equitable discretion to rescind its directive requiring PJM to update the historical tariff records (each of the Tariff, Schedule 12 Appendices that became effective on or after June 18, 2015), and make filings showing revised cost responsibility assignments.  PJM estimates that this review could require 19,000 pages of Tariff records review, that would take 2,900 hours at a cost of $419,920.  PJM argues that the historical changes to be filed with the Commission are entirely retrospective and would arguably only be practically beneficial for historical purposes.  PJM states that the equities weigh in favor of rescinding this requirement, and that PJM would commit to filing a refund report including each revised cost responsibility assignment on which the resettlements were based and/or PJM could post as publicly available the revised cost responsibility assignments. 
Commission Determination
On further consideration, we agree that the significant undertaking described by PJM to update its historical Tariff records outweighs the utility of developing historical Tariff records.  Therefore, we set the Order on Remand aside, in part, to rescind the directive requiring PJM to update the historical Tariff records (each of the Tariff, Schedule 12 Appendices that became effective on or after June 18, 2015) as directed in the Order on Remand.  
Clarification
Request for Clarification
PJM seeks clarification on a number of discrete issues that it claims are essential for it to accurately and equitably implement the directives of the Order on Remand.  PJM asserts that these clarifications are necessary to ensure that the compliance process is implemented in a technically sound, administratively manageable, and equitable manner. 
First, PJM seeks authorization to employ a simplified method for recalculating cost responsibility assignments.  PJM proposes to divide the refund period into two time periods:  the period June 18, 2015 through December 31, 2019, and January 1, 2020 to the present.  PJM claims that for the first phase, it would rely upon the power flow models/transmission system topology/datasets that were effective on December 31, 2019, and use that to update cost responsibility assignments removing the de minimis threshold back through June 18, 2015.  For the second group, PJM proposes to use the flow models/transmission system topology/datasets for each respective year.
PJM explains that reconstructing the underlying historical datasets and software tools for each interval is more difficult and time-consuming the further back in time it is extended.  PJM also explains that software may be obsolete or data formats could have changed.  PJM states that this method would still produce recalculated cost responsibility assignments that are reasonably accurate and would reduce the time of recalculation by one-third.  
Second, PJM requests confirmation that it is not required to update cost responsibility assignments—or revise any corresponding tariff records—for projects that have not yet entered service and lack Commission-authorized rate incentives for pre-service recovery.  PJM notes that of the 1,200 projects implicated by the directive of the Order on Remand, PJM is not billing for projects not yet in service, which totals over 600 projects.  PJM explains that preparing cost responsibility assignments for these projects will involve significant administrative burden but have no value because these cost responsibility assignments will have to be updated prior to the projects going into service.  PJM estimates that this approach will save between 2,640 – 4,752 hours of time in calculating updated cost responsibility assignments.
Third, PJM seeks clarification that it is authorized to assess and collect surcharges to recover prior-period under-allocations dating to June 18, 2015.  PJM notes that its existing tariff provisions restrict retroactive billing adjustments and that, as a not-for-profit entity, it cannot fund refunds absent the ability to issue surcharges.
Fourth, PJM asks the Commission to clarify that its refund obligations are strictly limited to the amounts actually collected through surcharges, emphasizing that PJM cannot distribute funds it does not receive and that any shortfall in surcharge collections should proportionally reduce the refunds owed to beneficiaries.  PJM asks the Commission to clarify that this obligation also extends to interest.
Fifth, PJM seeks guidance regarding whether current or historical load serving entities (LSEs) should be the subjects of resettlement billing.  PJM explains that many LSEs active earlier in the nearly 11-year period are no longer participating in PJM markets, creating significant collection challenges and the near-certainty of uncollectible amounts if historical LSEs must be pursued.  Accordingly, PJM recommends that the Commission authorize a settlement with a set of current “Responsible Customers” to ensure administrability and to reduce the risk of incomplete recovery.  PJM seeks clarification regarding which entities it should invoice.
Sixth, PJM states that, absent contrary direction, it interprets the compliance directive to encompass resettlements of Incremental Capacity Transfer Rights (ICTRs) and certain Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service charges and credits, because the allocations for these instruments are directly tied to the underlying project cost responsibility assignments and must therefore be revised in tandem.  PJM states that it intends to resettle any ICTRs associated with a project for which PJM is also rebilling.  PJM intends to resettle Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service invoices for merchant transmission facilities with Firm Transmission Withdrawal Rights.  PJM also seeks clarification that to the extent the resettlements affect a Transmission Owner’s Network Integration Transmission Service rate, whether a stated rate or formula, that rate may need to be adjusted correspondingly.  However, PJM states that whether any such changes to a transmission owner’s current or historical rate need to be made is beyond PJM’s purview.
Seventh, PJM requests clarification regarding whether the Order on Remand requires the resettlement of costs associated with Reliability-Must-Run (RMR) agreements, noting that these allocations are similarly dependent on the cost responsibility assignments of related transmission upgrades, but that many RMR cost allocations were established through settlements whose expectations could be disrupted by retrospective modification.

New York Entities state that in principle they do not oppose PJM’s simplified approach for recalculating the cost responsibility assignments for years 2015 through 2019 in PJM’s first clarification request, but call for more detail as to how this will be accomplished.  They state it is unclear how Con Edison, Linden, and Hudson will be included in certain power flow models and data sets under the simplified approach.

The New York Entities oppose PJM’s sixth clarification request interpreting the compliance directive to encompass resettlements of ICTRs and certain Firm Point-to-Point Transmission Service charges and credits.  They ask that the Commission clarify that PJM is not authorized to “resettle” ICTRs and Firm                        Point-to-Point transmission service invoices from 2015-2026.  They claim that “resettlement of ICTRs and Firm Point-to-Point transmission service charge/credits” was not previously raised in these proceedings and is outside the scope of the proceedings.
The New York Entities oppose PJM’s seventh clarification request regarding resettlement treatment of RMR agreements.  As with clarification six, the New York Entities state that resettling the RMR agreements is beyond the scope of these proceedings and should not be included in the resettlement process. 
Commission Determination
Among other things, the requested clarifications raise questions about the appropriate method for calculating updated cost responsibility assignments and raise concerns regarding PJM’s ability to recalculate cost allocations going back to June 2015, including but not limited to concerns regarding available modeling data.  We find that the details about how PJM should calculate updated cost responsibility assignments involve issues of material fact that cannot be resolved on the record before us and that are more appropriately addressed in the hearing and settlement judge procedures ordered below.  Accordingly, we establish hearing and settlement judge procedures to develop a further record to determine the method for calculating updated cost responsibility assignments and the appropriate amount of refunds and interest, consistent with our findings in this order.  We grant PJM’s second and third requested clarifications and include the remaining clarification requests within the hearing and settlement procedures ordered below.
First, we grant PJM’s requested clarification that it is not required to update cost responsibility assignments—or revise any corresponding tariff records—for projects that have not yet entered service and lack Commission-authorized rate incentives for pre-service recovery.  As PJM explains, transmission owners do not begin recovering costs associated with these facilities until they are placed in service, and updating illustrative, preliminary cost assignments for those facilities would require a significant time expenditure with limited benefit.  Consistent with our finding above that PJM need not update historical tariff records because of the associated burden, we grant this requested clarification.
We also grant PJM’s clarification request that the Commission confirm PJM is authorized to assess and collect surcharges to recover prior-period under-allocations dating to June 18, 2015.  Given that we reaffirm our refund directives in this order, we also affirm PJM’s authority to effectuate those refunds via surcharges.   
While we are setting these matters for a trial-type evidentiary hearing, we encourage efforts to reach settlement before hearing procedures commence.  To aid settlement efforts, we will hold the hearing in abeyance and direct that a settlement judge be appointed, pursuant to Rule 603 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure.  If parties desire, they may, by mutual agreement, request a specific judge as the settlement judge in the proceeding.  The Chief Judge, however, may not be able to designate the requested settlement judge based on workload requirements which determine judges’ availability.  The settlement judge shall report to the Chief Judge and the Commission within 30 days of the date of the appointment of the settlement judge on the status of settlement discussions.  Based on this report, the Chief Judge shall provide additional time to continue settlement discussions or provide for commencement of a hearing by assigning the case to a presiding judge.
As discussed above, the Commission granted a request by PJM for additional time “to recalculate the cost allocations in Schedule 12 and correct the billing (with interest calculated pursuant to section 35.19(a) of the Commission regulations)” within 90 days of the issuance of the Order on Remand for all projects subject to the solution-based DFAX cost allocation method back to June 18, 2015, “to make cleanup filings through eTariff to correct the cost allocations for each cost allocation,” and to refile revised, historical versions of Schedule 12 of the Tariff until further order of the Commission.  Because we are now setting these issues for hearing and settlement judge procedures, we accordingly continue to extend PJM’s time to comply with the compliance directive until further order of the Commission.
Short Circuit Issues
Background
In the Order on Remand, the Commission established a paper hearing to obtain additional record evidence to address the concerns raised in the Remand Opinion regarding the application of the solution-based DFAX method to short circuit reliability violations.  
Specifically, the Commission sought comment on whether the existing rate, which allocates either 50% or 100% of the costs of facilities addressing short circuit violations based on modeled power flows/usage during steady-state conditions under the                     solution-based DFAX method, is unjust and unreasonable and whether short circuit projects should be treated similarly to stability by allocating their costs using a method that is not based on modeled power flows/usage during steady-state conditions.
The Commission requested that parties address whether the solution-based DFAX method is just and reasonable for allocation of the costs of transmission projects to resolve short circuit reliability issues.  Particularly, the Commission sought additional information on whether the costs allocated to zones for transmission facilities that address short-circuit reliability violations under the solution-based DFAX method are roughly commensurate with the benefits derived by zones that contributed to the underlying      short-circuit reliability violations and/or use the subject transmission projects.
The Commission requested that parties address whether there are differences between transmission projects that address stability and short circuit violations that make the solution-based DFAX method appropriate to use to allocate some or all of the costs of transmission facilities selected in the RTEP to address short circuit violations even though the reliability issues are not based on power flows during steady-state conditions.
In addition, in the event that parties maintain that solution-based DFAX cost allocation for transmission projects that resolve short circuit violations is unjust and unreasonable, the Commission requested that parties address potential replacement rates – that is, other potential cost allocation methods for such projects that align with the cost causation principle.  For example, the Commission sought comment on potential approaches that would allocate the costs of short circuit projects to the loads that would be most impacted by an unresolved short circuit violation and therefore would benefit from transmission facilities that address the short circuit reliability issue.  The Commission also sought comment on the extent to which alternative methods allocate costs based on benefits at a single point in time or reflect changing use of the transmission system.
Procedural Issues
Initial comments in the short circuit paper hearing proceeding established in the Order on Remand were filed by PJM, PJM Indicated Transmission Owners, PSEG, and the New York Entities and were due on June 4, 2026.  Reply briefs were filed by the    New York Entities, PJM, and PJM Indicated Transmission Owners on August 3, 2026.  On August 31, 2026, PJM filed an answer to the New York Entities’ reply briefs.  On September 28, 2026, the New York Entities filed an answer to PJM’s supplemental reply.  Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure prohibits an answer to an answer unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept all answers regarding the application of the solution-based DFAX method to short circuit reliability violations paper hearing proceeding so they can become part of the record as we are setting this issue for hearing and settlement judge procedures. 
Commission Determination
As discussed above, we are setting the issues of material fact related to the method for calculating updated cost responsibility assignments and the appropriate amount of refunds and interest for hearing and settlement judge procedures because PJM does not have modeling data that permits it to calculate refunds accurately, and PJM has requested several clarifications whose implications for accurate calculation we cannot resolve without a more fulsome record.  We also are setting issues of material fact regarding the application of the solution-based DFAX method to short circuit reliability violations for hearing and settlement judge procedures.  After reviewing the pleadings in the paper hearing, we continue to have concerns as to whether the solution-based DFAX method is a just and reasonable allocation mechanism for transmission facilities that address short circuit violations.  For example, because the record is unclear about which parties are affected by short-circuit violations, identifying the beneficiaries of the transmission facilities that address the short circuit reliability issues is correspondingly difficult and a further factual record is needed to make this determination.  Moreover, because the resolution of the short circuit issue may create the same refund and surcharge issues as the de minimis threshold, hearing and settlement judge procedures would be necessary to determine refunds should the solution-based DFAX be found unjust and unreasonable.  For these reasons, we conclude that the most administratively efficient approach to resolving the short circuit issues is to include them as part of the hearing and settlement judge procedures directed in this order.  The paper hearing briefs submitted by parties, as supplemented by the further record developed by the presiding judge, should be incorporated into the hearing and settlement judge proceeding record.
